title: Quality assurance & image grading
blurb: The A/N image quality scale and its targets, the reject log, six-monthly image audits and the routine checks that keep radiography safe and consistent.
question: Your practice manager asks you to help with the six-monthly radiograph audit. Out of 100 digital intraoral images, 91 were graded 'A' and 9 'N', and most of the N images were bitewings with overlapped contacts taken by one new team member. Does the practice meet the target, and what should happen next?

teach.body: Quality assurance (QA) is the practice's planned system of checks that makes sure every radiograph is good enough to diagnose from, at the lowest sensible dose. The employer must have a written QA programme. It covers the X-ray equipment, receptors and processing, viewing conditions, staff training and, above all, the quality of the images themselves. Done well, QA spots problems early, before they turn into a run of retakes and extra dose for patients.

bands.label: Diagnostically acceptable
bands.sub: No or minimal errors; good enough to answer the clinical question

bands.label: Diagnostically not acceptable
bands.sub: Errors in preparation, exposure, positioning, processing or reconstruction make it unusable

teach.caption: This two-point scale was introduced in the 2020 Guidance Notes for Dental Practitioners and applies to all dental radiography, including CBCT.

items.label: graded A for digital images (N no more than 5%)
graded A for film images (N no more than 10%)
maximum interval between image quality analyses
minimum sample size, unless workload is too low

teach.caption: Practices treating particular groups, such as patients with additional needs, may set their own targets with their MPE and document why.

teach.body: A trained, experienced operator grades images either as they are viewed (prospective) or by pulling a representative sample from the records (retrospective). Results are analysed at least every six months, with a sample of at least 100 images where possible, and reported separately for each type of imaging, such as intraoral and panoramic. Image quality rating is not the same as clinical evaluation: rating judges whether the picture is technically good enough; evaluation is the dentist's interpretation of what it shows.

teach.caption: 91% is below the 95% digital target. The pattern (overlapped contacts, one operator) points to a cause: horizontal angulation, so the action is training and use of holders, then re-audit.

teach.h: Record for every 'N' image (the reject log)
items: The nature of the fault, for example overlapped contacts or cone cut.
How many repeat images were taken, if any.

teach.caption: Actions might be extra training, introducing holders, changing a procedure, or repairing equipment. The analysis and the action taken are both recorded.

head: Check
How often
rows: Review of the whole QA programme
Regularly, as set in the QA programme
teach.caption: Clinical audits must also cover justification and clinical evaluation of radiographs. Records of QA checks and audits are recommended to be kept for at least five years.

teach.text: The old 3-point scale (grades 1, 2 and 3) was REPLACED in 2020 by the 2-point A/N scale. Targets: A ≥ 95% digital, A ≥ 90% film. Don't mix the two systems in an exam answer.

items: Grade images A (diagnostically acceptable) or N (not acceptable).
Targets: A at least 95% for digital, 90% for film.
Analyse at least every 6 months, ideally 100+ images, separately for each modality.
Log every N image with date, fault, cause and repeats; look for trends and act, e.g. training and holders.

summary: You can now grade images with the A/N scale, quote the digital and film targets, describe how and how often image quality is audited, keep a reject log, use the audit cycle to fix a rising retake rate, and list the other routine QA checks.

A.q: Under current UK guidance, what is the target proportion of digital radiographs graded 'A'?
A.why: The 2020 guidance sets a target of at least 95% 'A' for digital imaging.

whyNot.0: 80% is below both the digital and film targets.
whyNot.1: At least 90% is the target for film, not digital.
whyNot.3: 70% is far below any current target.

A.q: What do the grades 'A' and 'N' stand for in image quality rating?
A.why: 'A' is diagnostically acceptable and 'N' is diagnostically not acceptable.

whyNot.2: The grades describe quality, not the type of receptor.
whyNot.3: 'Needs review' isn't part of the official scale.

A.q: A practice audit shows a rising number of retakes for periapicals. Which action best addresses this?
options: Increase the exposure settings on all units
A.why: Most retakes come from positioning errors; holders with beam-aiming devices and technique training reduce them.

whyNot.0: Higher exposures add dose and don't fix positioning faults.
whyNot.1: Periapicals are still needed when justified.
whyNot.3: Changing grades hides the problem rather than solving it.

B.q: How often should the practice analyse its image quality ratings?
B.why: Guidance recommends image quality and reject analysis at least once every six months.

whyNot.0: Monthly is not the guidance interval, although it wouldn't be wrong to do more.
whyNot.1: Three years is the interval for equipment tests and QA programme review.
whyNot.2: Audit is routine, not triggered only by complaints.

B.q: What was replaced by the A/N rating scale in the 2020 guidance?
B.why: The 2020 Guidance Notes replaced the older three-point scale with the two-point A/N scale.

whyNot.1: There was never a 10-point national scale for dental images.
whyNot.2: Image rating is not an exam.
whyNot.3: No colour-coded system was used for dental image grading.

B.q: What is the target proportion of 'A' grades for FILM radiographs?
B.why: For film, the target is at least 90% 'A' and no more than 10% 'N'.

whyNot.1: At least 95% is the digital target.

C.q: Which detail should be recorded in the reject log for an 'N' image?
options: The suspected cause of the fault
The cost of the patient's appointment
C.why: The log records the date, the nature of the fault, its known or suspected cause and the number of repeats.

whyNot.0: Home address isn't needed for fault analysis.
whyNot.2: The GDC number isn't part of the reject log.
whyNot.3: Cost has no bearing on image quality analysis.

C.q: What is the main purpose of routine quality assurance in radiography?
C.why: QA ensures images are consistently diagnostic at the lowest sensible dose and picks up faults early.

whyNot.0: QA has nothing to do with staffing levels.
whyNot.1: Clinical evaluation is a separate, required step.
whyNot.2: Registration with HSE is a legal requirement regardless of QA.

C.q: An audit of 100 digital images finds 93 graded A. What should the practice conclude?
options: It exceeds the film target, so is fine
C.why: 93% is below the 95% digital target, so the causes should be investigated and acted on.

whyNot.1: The digital target is at least 95%.
whyNot.2: These are digital images, so the film target doesn't apply.
whyNot.3: Missing the target means investigating and taking corrective action.

reteach.title: Like a driving test for images
reteach.question: If each radiograph sat a driving test, what would 'pass' and 'fail' mean, and what would the instructor do if lots of pupils failed for the same reason?

blocks.h: Pass, fail, and fixing the pattern
blocks.body: Each image either passes (A: it can answer the clinical question) or fails (N: it can't). The practice needs at least 95 in every 100 digital images to pass, or 90 in 100 for film. If lots fail for the same reason, a good instructor doesn't just shrug: they look at the reject log, spot that most failures are, say, overlapped contacts from one person, and give targeted coaching. Six months later they check again.

steps.label: Spot the pattern
steps.sub: Same fault, view, machine or person?

blocks.text: Grading is about technical quality, not about the diagnosis. A perfect 'A' image can still show disease, and a healthy mouth can still produce an 'N' image.

explain.body: A = diagnostically acceptable: no or minimal errors and good enough to answer the clinical question. N = not acceptable: errors make it unusable. It replaced the old 1/2/3 scale in 2020.

test.q: A bitewing has a small cone cut at one corner, but every contact and tooth needed is clearly visible. How should it be graded?
options: N, because there is a visible fault
A, because it is still diagnostic
test.why: 'A' allows minimal errors as long as the image answers the clinical question.

whyNot.0: N is for errors that make the image diagnostically unacceptable.
whyNot.2: The old 1/2/3 scale is no longer used.
whyNot.3: A diagnostic image should not be retaken.

explain.body: Digital: at least 95% A. Film: at least 90% A. Analyse at least every six months, using at least 100 images if possible, separately for each type of imaging.

test.q: A practice uses both intraoral and panoramic imaging. How should the audit results be reported?
test.why: Where more than one modality is used, results should be reported separately for each.

whyNot.1: Combining hides problems in one modality.
whyNot.2: Panoramic images must be audited too.
whyNot.3: Audits use a representative sample, not just the worst period.

explain.body: For every N image, record the date, the fault, its known or suspected cause and any repeats. Review the log at each six-monthly analysis, look for patterns by procedure, equipment or person, and record what you did about them.

test.q: The reject log shows most N images come from one X-ray unit. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Ignore it until the next audit
test.why: A pattern linked to one unit suggests an equipment problem, which should be investigated and repaired, then recorded.

whyNot.0: Trends should be acted on, not left.
whyNot.1: Targets can't be lowered to hide an equipment fault.
whyNot.2: Raising exposures adds dose and doesn't fix the cause.

explain.body: Light-boxes and viewing conditions at least every six months; X-ray equipment routine tests at least every three years; the whole QA programme reviewed at least every three years; receptors inspected regularly.

test.q: How often should X-ray equipment have its routine performance test?
test.why: Routine tests of dental X-ray equipment are carried out at least every three years, and after any significant change.

whyNot.0: Monthly testing isn't the guidance interval for equipment.
whyNot.1: Six months is the interval for image audits and viewing checks.
whyNot.3: Testing is planned and routine, not just after faults.
